20 BACKGROUND
21 The Twin Rivers Unified School District ("District") and the Twin Rivers United Educators
22 ("Association") are parties to a collective bargaining agreement. The parties began successor negotiations on
23 February 27, 2025 and met 11 times. In the course of negotiations the parties reached agreement on eight contract
24 articles but were unable to resolve their differences on another 16. The fmal negotiation session took place on
25 October 27, 2025 and on October 28 the Association filed a Request for Impasse Determination/Assignment with
26 the Public Employment Relations Board ("PERB").

13 STATUTORY CRITERIA
14 California Government Code Section 3548.2 requires the Factfinding Panel to apply the following criteria
15 in making its recommendations:
16 1. State and federal laws that are applicable to the employer.
17 2. Stipulations of the parties.
18 3. The interests and welfare of the public and the fmancial ability of the public school employer.
19 4. Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of the employees involved in the
20 factfinding proceeding with the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of other employees
21 performing similar services and with other employees generally in public school employment in
22 comparable communities.
23 5. The consumer price index for good and services, commonly known as the cost ofliving.
24 6. The overall compensation presently received by the employees, including direct wage compensation,
25 vacations, holidays, and other excused time, insurance and pensions, medical and hospitalization

1 INFORMATION PRESENTED DURING FACTFINDING
2 The panel considered all the information provided by the parties. Given the volume, depth, and level of
3 detail, it is not practicable to discuss every piece of information and argument presented during factfinding, but the
4 decision not to mention any given information in this report does not imply that it was overlooked or not considered.
5 The Twin Rivers Unified School District is a public school employer within the meaning of California
6 Government Code Section 3540.l(k). It serves over 24,000 students in northern Sacramento County in grades Pre-
7 kindergarten through 12. It is the fourth largest school district in Sacramento County and the 27th largest in the state.
8 The District includes 18 preschool sites, 27 elementary schools, five junior high schools, four senior high schools,
9 three charter schools, two continuation high schools, a special education school, an independent study K-12 school,
10 and an adult education program. Its average daily attendance ("ADA") for 2024-25 was 20,717. Its total operating
11 revenues for 2024-25 were approximately $562 million.
12 State and Federal Laws Awlicable to the Emplqyer
13 The District receives most of its revenue from the state according to the Local Control Funding Formula
14 ("LCFF"). Under the LCFF, the District receives a base grant tied to the average daily attendance of pupils as well
15 as supplemental and concentration grants based on the unduplicated pupil percentage ("UPP"), i.e., the percentage o
16 district students who are eligible for free or reduced price meals, English learners, or foster youth. ( CCR Title 5,
17 section 15495(m)). Supplemental and concentration grants are subject to various requirements including a Local
18 Control and Accountability Plan ("LCAP") addressing the use of the funds to improve services for high-needs
19 students. (CCR Title 5, section 15494). The District has a UPP of over 90%, which entitles it to spend the
20 supplemental and concentration grants district-wide. (Educ. Code section 42238.07, CCR Title 5 section
21 15496(b)(l)).
22 Education Code section 41372 requires school districts to spend at least 55% of their educational budgets
23 on teacher salaries (including health and welfare benefits), unless they obtain a waiver from the County Office of
24 Education. Waivers may be granted on the basis of "serious hardship" or if a district demonstrates that it
25 compensates teachers at a higher rate than comparable jurisdictions.
26 School districts are required to maintain a minimum unrestricted reserve of at least 3%. For fiscal years
27 where the state Public School System Stabilization Account meets a certain threshold, Education Code section
28 42127.0l(e) provides that district budgets "shall not contain a combined assigned or unassigned ending general fund

7 The Interests and Welfare ofthe Public and the Financial Ability ofthe Employer
8 In support of its proposals to increase pay and benefits and limit class sizes, the Association points to the 83
9 current vacancies in the bargaining unit and argues that teachers are leaving the District to take jobs in better paying
10 districts such as Sacramento City Unified. It argues that the District's turnover rate of9% in 2023-24 and 10.8% in
11 2024-25 far exceeds the District's goal ofretaining 95% of certificated staff. Association members spoke about a
12 particularly acute shortage of teachers in the special education area, which they argue has led to gaps in services, a
13 lack of continuity, overly heavy caseloads, and over reliance on outside contractors. Association members noted the
14 heavy burden of dependent health care coverage, which under the current CBA language costs members from
15 $2,000 to over $15,000 per year. Teachers also spoke about the importance, as spelled out in the District's LCAP, of
16 smaller class sizes, and the need for more prep time for elementary school teachers.
17 The Association points to several factors in support of its argument that the District can afford the cost of
18 its proposals. First, the District has a reserve fund balance of 13%, which is significantly higher than the amount
19 required by state law and may be subject to the requirement that it spend down uncommitted reserve funds over 10¾
20 when the reserve cap is triggered by the state. Second, the Association argues that the District has repeatedly fallen
21 short of the Education Code section 41372(b)(3) requirement that it spend 55% of its current education expenses on
22 salaries of classroom teachers, a difference of $13 million for the current fiscal year and a total of $116 million since
23 2019-20. Third, the high percentage of UPP means that the District receives significantly more in state funding per
24 student than other districts. Fourth, the Association points to the District's decision to put $267 million in
25 unrestricted funds into a Fund 40, a capital improvements fund, and to budget additional contributions to that fund
26 through 2027-28. Finally, the Association points to an additional $36 million in additional funds (most of which is
27 one-time money) in the Governor's proposed budget.

9 District salaries have kept pace - almost exactly -with both COLA and CPI increases in the past five years.
10 District employees are well situated compared to those in comparable districts with respect to salary, neither

17 pay the proposed full coverage of health benefits at the Kaiser family rate during the term of the CBA, which would

19 ongoing basis without caps presents a significant risk given the unpredictable and often precipitous escalation of

FACTFINDING PANEL REPORT- 13

Dissent and Partial Concurrence Regarding the TRUE-TRUSD Fact-Finding
Report, March 2, 2026
"Our mission isn't to save money, ... it is to create a stable environment. ... [C]lassroom teachers
instability causes them to constantly look around them as opposed to being focused on their
classroom."
Mike Fine, CEO California's Fiscal Crisis Management Assistance Team, February 26, 2026, Ed
Source Roundtable, "Teachers on strike: Can school districts in California afford what teachers
want?"
#
Instead of bringing the parties closer together, the fact-finder's report makes a strike
inevitable.
The fact-finder's report fails to address any of the serious concerns raised by educators,
takes no meaningful steps to ensure that Twin Rivers classrooms are fully-funded, and
recommends the continuation of the status quo that every day leaves two thousand Twin
Rivers Unified School District students without a permanent credentialed educator
providing instructional services.
The fact-finder's recommendation completely fails to address this crisis and makes no
contribution to averting the strike.
For the last six years, the District's outside independent auditor has cited TRUSD in its annual
audited report for its failure to comply with California Ed Code that requires unified school districts
to spend 55% of their annual budget on classroom staff. For six years, TRUSD has defied those
recommendations, diverting $116 million, or an average of over $19 million per year, away from
classrooms. The fact-finder was made aware of this non-compliance but her recommendation fails
to factor in those millions of dollars as statute requires her to con ·id r in order to fully fund
classrooms and address the concerns of students and staff.
TRUE has proposed numerous improvements, including lowering class sizes, reduced caseloads and
improved services for students with disabilities, overages for when class sizes and caseloads are
exceeded, an end to reliance on outside contractors, the reduction of unnecessary testing, the use of
Al, increased prep time for elementary teachers, an end to practices which expand educators' work
day without compensation, and protections for personal and academic freedom. The fact-finder's
recommendation addresses almost none of these proposals, recommending largely the status quo on
all articles except wages and medical insurance. And even in those limited areas where something
other than the status quo is recommended, the improvement is limited.
A full year after negotiations began, Twin Rivers educators represented by the Twin Rivers United
Educators (TRUE) believe that a contract negotiated with Twin Rivers Unified School District
1

should reflect the same significant improvements achieved by the Sacramento City Teachers
Association in June 2025, the United Teachers of Richmond in December 2025, the United
Educators of San Francisco in February 2026, the San Diego Education Association in February
2026, and the Oakland Education Association in March 2026.
Unfortunately, the neutral has chosen not to be informed by those agreements which establish and
consolidate new standards for educators across the state of California, thereby largely disregarding
applicable criteria, notably state law applicable to the employer and the interests and welfare of the
public and financial ability of the public-school employer. In her zeal to accept the austerity
arguments of the TRUSD, she even recommended a first-year salary increase lower than the
proposal TRUSD currently has on the table.
It is without argument that Twin Rivers Unified School District is
one of the strongest financially-positioned school districts in the
state of California. The fact-finder operates as if TRUSD is on the
verge of insolvency.
• TRUSD is One of the Small Number of Districts Where Enrollment/A DA is
Growing and Has the Second Highest Rate of Enrollment Growth for Comparable
Districts
Across California, 2/3 of all school districts are experiencing long-term enrollment decline.
Twin Rivers is an exception. From 2021-22 through 2024-25 for which data is available, out
of 44 unified school districts in California with an ADA of 20,000 students or more, Twin
Rivers is one of only eleven where enrollment has increased over the past five years. Out of
those 44 districts, Twin Rivers' enrollment growth ranks number five. The number of
students enrolled in Twin Rivers Unified has increased from 23,904 in 2021-22 to 25,164 in
2025-26, an increase of 1,260 students or 5.3%.
• TRUSD has failed to meet the Ed Code 41372 that unified school districts spend 55%
of their budget on classrooms since 2019-20, and is a massive outlier. The District
failed to address the fact that the failure in 2024-25 was the sixth year in a row that the
District failed to spend the required 55%, totaling $116 million since 2019-20 diverting the
money to its unrestricted reserve fund and its special Fund 40 (see below). The District also
failed to disclose that in each of those years, the District's own independent auditors
recommended that the District correct the deficiency, a recommendation that the District
repeatedly ignores. Of the 44 comparator school districts, TRUSD is one of only four that
failed to meet the requirement in 2024-25.
2

• TRUSD has one of the highest Unduplicated Pupil Populations (UPP) in the state,
resulting in LCFF funding that exceeds $3500 per student - higher than other
Sacramento County districts and the median of unified school districts with ADA
over 20,000 students. These funds are meant to improve outcomes of "high needs"
students including English Learners, low-income, and foster youth. The District has the
means to fill vacancies, retain educators, and reduce class sizes cuts for Sacramento's most
underserved students and families.
• TRUSD has failed to provide salary increases to certificated staff that have kept pace
with District LCFF revenue increases. Salary increases to the TRUE bargaining unit
salary schedules have not kept pace with the District's increase in LCFF revenue. Since
2020-21, the District's LCFF revenue has increased by a cumulative 35.3%, while salary
schedules have only increased by a cumulative 23.8%, a gap of 11.5%.
• TRUSD's unrestricted reserve fund exceeds the 10% maximum reserve fund
currently in effect for California school districts by $19.5 million. Based on the
